title: On the Use of Windows for Harmonic Analysis with the Discrete Fourier Transform
access: full (complete 33-page scanned article openly hosted in Carnegie Mellon University course materials; Proceedings of the IEEE, vol. 66, no. 1, January 1978, journal pp. 51–83; the first page states ‘U.S. Government work not protected by U.S. copyright’)
topics: Abstract and §I Introduction (journal p. 51; PDF p. 1): window effects on detection and estimation, especially weak tones in broadband noise or near strong harmonics; finite observation, sampled data, and the DFT as practical constraints.

§II Harmonic Analysis of Finite-Extent Data and the DFT (journal pp. 51–52; PDF pp. 1–2): orthogonal sinusoidal bases, N samples over a half-open NT-second interval, periodic extension, DFT-even symmetry, and the missing endpoint.

§III Spectral Leakage (journal pp. 52–53; PDF pp. 2–3): off-bin tones, boundary discontinuities in periodic extension, leakage as a finite-record effect rather than a sampling effect, and windows as boundary smoothers or modified basis vectors.

§IV Windows and Figures of Merit (journal pp. 53–58; PDF pp. 3–8): multiplication by a window as spectral convolution, finite Fourier transform versus DFT conventions, phase shifts from changing the time origin, and comparative performance criteria.
§IV.A Equivalent Noise Bandwidth (journal p. 54; PDF p. 4): a window as a spectral filter and ENBW as the equal-peak-gain rectangular bandwidth that admits the same broadband-noise power.

§IV.B Processing Gain (journal pp. 54–56; PDF pp. 4–6): the DFT as a matched-filter bank, coherent versus incoherent gain, window-induced processing loss, and the reciprocal relation between processing gain and normalized ENBW.

§IV.C Overlap Correlation (journal pp. 56–57; PDF pp. 6–7): resolution bandwidth, partition overlap, correlation of adjacent windowed transforms, and variance reduction when averaging correlated spectral estimates.
§IV.D–E Scalloping Loss and Worst-Case Processing Loss (journal p. 57; PDF p. 7): the picket-fence effect for a half-bin tone and the combined loss from windowing plus worst-case frequency placement.

§IV.F Spectral Leakage Revisited (journal pp. 57–58; PDF pp. 7–8): main-lobe concentration, peak sidelobe level, sidelobe falloff, amplitude/frequency bias, self-leakage between positive- and negative-frequency kernels, and weak-tone masking.

§IV.G Minimum Resolution Bandwidth (journal pp. 57–58; PDF pp. 7–8): why coherent DFT resolution is governed by 6 dB rather than 3 dB bandwidth, and a normalized ENBW-minus-3 dB bandwidth diagnostic for window quality.

§V.A Rectangle (Dirichlet) Window (journal pp. 58–59; PDF pp. 8–9): gating, Dirichlet-kernel transform, narrow main lobe, high sidelobes, 6 dB/octave falloff, partial Fourier sums, and Gibbs oscillation.

§V.B Triangle (Fejér/Bartlett) Window (journal pp. 59–60; PDF pp. 9–10): self-convolution of rectangles, squared Dirichlet transform, doubled roots, nonnegative spectrum, 12 dB/octave falloff, and Cesàro/Fejér averaging of partial sums.

§V.C cos^α(X) Windows (journal pp. 60–62; PDF pp. 10–12): cosine powers α=1–4, smoothness versus main-lobe width, the Hann window, cancellation among three shifted Dirichlet kernels, and economical frequency-domain implementation.

§V.D Hamming Window (journal pp. 62–63; PDF pp. 12–13): coefficient adjustment to cancel the first sidelobe, the distinction between exact cancellation and the conventional 0.54/0.46 coefficients, low first sidelobe but slow asymptotic falloff.

§V.E Blackman Window (journal pp. 63–65; PDF pp. 13–15): three shifted kernels, exact versus rounded Blackman coefficients, boundary smoothness, gradient-designed three- and four-term Blackman–Harris families, and short spectral-convolution implementations.

§V.F Constructed Windows (journal pp. 65–69; PDF pp. 15–19): Riesz, Riemann, de la Vallée-Poussin, Tukey, Bohman, Poisson, Hann–Poisson, and Cauchy constructions, with their smoothness, sidelobe, and bandwidth consequences.

§V.G Gaussian/Weierstrass Window (journal pp. 69–71; PDF pp. 19–21): uncertainty-product motivation, truncation, parameterized exchange of main-lobe width for boundary discontinuity and sidelobe level.

§V.H Dolph–Chebyshev Window (journal pp. 71–73; PDF pp. 21–23): minimax/equiripple sidelobes, minimum main-lobe width for a specified sidelobe level, discrete construction through transform samples, and endpoint impulses.
§V.I Kaiser–Bessel Window (journal p. 73; PDF p. 23): approximation to the order-zero prolate-spheroidal solution that maximizes in-band energy for fixed time duration and energy.
§V.J Barcilon–Temes Window (journal pp. 73–76; PDF pp. 23–26): weighted out-of-band-energy minimization and performance between the Dolph–Chebyshev and Kaiser–Bessel criteria.

§VI Harmonic Analysis (journal pp. 76–81; PDF pp. 26–31): a controlled two-tone experiment sweeping window families to compare detection of a −40 dB tone 5.5 bins from a strong tone, resolution nulls, artifacts, and leakage floors.

§VII Conclusions (journal pp. 81–82; PDF pp. 31–32): windows are similar for a single tone in broadband noise but dramatically different for unequal nearby tones; Kaiser–Bessel and Blackman–Harris emerge as practical top performers.
Appendix (journal p. 83; PDF p. 33): derivation that time-domain windowing is convolution by the window transform in frequency.

References and additional general references (journal p. 83; PDF p. 33): foundational sources on spectral estimation, Fourier convergence, optimal windows, prolate-spheroidal functions, and Welch averaging.
key_results: §II (journal pp. 51–52; PDF pp. 1–2): an N-sample DFT record represents a half-open interval; the sample at the omitted right endpoint is identified with the first sample of the next periodic extension. DFT-even therefore means zero projection on sampled sine sequences, not conventional point-for-point symmetry about the midpoint.

§II, Figs. 1–3 (journal p. 52; PDF p. 2): a conventionally even finite sequence with the right endpoint deleted can have a continuous finite transform with an imaginary component while its DFT samples are purely real, because the DFT samples land on zeros of the missing-endpoint sinusoid.

§III (journal pp. 52–53; PDF pp. 2–3): only tones coincident with the finite-record sinusoidal basis project onto one basis vector; every off-bin tone projects across the basis. Leakage is caused by finite-duration observation, not by sampling.

§III (journal pp. 52–53; PDF pp. 2–3): the periodic extension of a noncommensurate sinusoid has boundary discontinuities. Tapering reduces leakage by forcing the weighted data and, where possible, successive derivatives toward matching boundary values.

§IV, eqs. (5)–(6) (journal p. 53; PDF p. 3): multiplying sampled data by w(nT) makes the observed spectrum F_w(ω)=F(ω)*W(ω); each estimate is therefore a weighted accumulation of contributions from surrounding frequencies.

§IV (journal p. 53; PDF p. 3): shifting a centered window by N/2 samples changes transform phase. Omitting that shift—especially when applying a window as spectral convolution—is a major source of wrong signs and window misapplication.

§IV.A, eqs. (8)–(11) (journal p. 54; PDF p. 4): normalized equivalent noise bandwidth is ENBW = N·Σ_n w²[n]/(Σ_n w[n])², measured in DFT bins. It is the width of an equal-peak-gain rectangular filter passing the same white-noise power.

§IV.B, eqs. (13)–(15) (journal pp. 54–56; PDF pp. 4–6): coherent signal gain is Σw[n], incoherent white-noise power gain is σ²Σw²[n], and processing gain is (Σw[n])²/Σw²[n]; normalized processing gain is the reciprocal of ENBW.
§IV.C, eq. (16) (journal p. 56; PDF p. 6): practical resolution bandwidth is Δf=βf_s/N, with β commonly chosen as the window ENBW in bins rather than treating f_s/N alone as the resolution.

§IV.C, eqs. (17)–(19) (journal pp. 56–57; PDF pp. 6–7): overlap correlation is the normalized inner product of shifted windows. It determines the actual variance reduction when averaging overlapped transforms; for good windows, 50%-overlapped transforms are nearly independent.

§IV.D, eq. (20) (journal p. 57; PDF p. 7): scalloping loss is the ratio of coherent gain for a tone halfway between bins to coherent gain for a bin-centered tone, and is the maximum extra loss due solely to tone location relative to the DFT grid.

§IV.E (journal p. 57; PDF p. 7): worst-case processing loss is window processing loss plus maximum scalloping loss. Across the catalog it lies roughly between 3.0 and 4.3 dB; Harris calls values above 3.8 dB very poor.

§IV.E (journal p. 57; PDF p. 7): for detecting one tone in broadband noise, nearly every nonrectangular window differs by less than 1 dB, and good windows by less than 0.7 dB; window choice matters much more for a weak tone near a strong tone.

§IV.F (journal pp. 57–58; PDF pp. 7–8): weak-tone dynamic range depends on both peak sidelobe level and asymptotic sidelobe falloff. Leakage also biases the apparent amplitude and frequency of a single real sinusoid through interaction between its positive- and negative-frequency kernels.

§IV.G (journal p. 58; PDF p. 8): two equal coherent kernels require each contribution at the crossover to be below one half the peak, so 6 dB bandwidth—not the usual 3 dB bandwidth—defines minimum two-line resolution in the windowed DFT.

§IV.G (journal p. 58; PDF p. 8): the ratio (ENBW−3 dB bandwidth)/(3 dB bandwidth) is 4.0–5.5% for the paper’s good windows; values outside that band flag either an excessively wide main lobe or excessive sidelobe energy.

§V.A (journal pp. 58–59; PDF pp. 8–9): the rectangular window has a two-bin zero-to-zero main lobe, first sidelobe about −13 dB, and 6 dB/octave sidelobe falloff; it is narrow but poor at suppressing nearby components.

§V.B (journal pp. 59–60; PDF pp. 9–10): the triangular window transform is the squared Dirichlet kernel, with twice the rectangular main-lobe width, about −26/−27 dB first sidelobe, and 12 dB/octave falloff.

§V.B (journal pp. 59–60; PDF pp. 9–10): self-convolving a parent window doubles transform zeros at existing locations rather than placing them near sidelobe maxima, so the extra polynomial order is inefficient if the objective is minimum sidelobes.

§V.C, eqs. (28)–(29), Fig. 20 (journal pp. 61–62; PDF pp. 11–12): the Hann transform is a sum of three shifted Dirichlet kernels whose sidelobes cancel. On the DFT grid it can be applied by the three-point spectral convolution F_H[k]=0.5F[k]−0.25(F[k−1]+F[k+1]).

§V.C (journal p. 62; PDF p. 12): the alternating signs in Hann spectral convolution come from the shifted time origin; using all-positive coefficients is incorrect for DFT processing even though that error appears in literature and practice.

§V.D (journal pp. 62–63; PDF pp. 12–13): setting the Hamming constant to 25/46 exactly cancels the first sidelobe; the conventional 0.54/0.46 approximation gives about −42 dB initial sidelobes but a boundary discontinuity and only 6 dB/octave asymptotic decay.

§V.E (journal pp. 63–65; PDF pp. 13–15): rounded Blackman coefficients 0.42, 0.50, 0.08 sum to zero at the boundary and produce 18 dB/octave falloff and about −58 dB peak sidelobes; the ‘exact’ coefficients do not vanish at the boundary and fall only 6 dB/octave despite about −51 dB peak sidelobes.

§V.E (journal pp. 64–65; PDF pp. 14–15): gradient-designed minimum three- and four-term Blackman–Harris windows reach about −67 dB and −92 dB peak sidelobes, respectively; a selected four-term variant trades some sidelobe depth for better two-tone behavior.

§V.F (journal pp. 65–69; PDF pp. 15–19): smoothness at the record boundary predicts far-sidelobe decay: a discontinuity in the function yields 1/ω, in the first derivative 1/ω², and so on. Constructed windows can therefore be screened by endpoint derivative continuity before detailed testing.

§V.G, eq. (43) (journal pp. 69–71; PDF pp. 19–21): all functions satisfy the mean-square time-bandwidth inequality TW≥1/(4π), with equality only for the Gaussian; truncating its tails sacrifices exact optimality but retains a useful concentration tradeoff.

§V.H (journal pp. 71–73; PDF pp. 21–23): the discrete Dolph–Chebyshev window minimizes main-lobe width for a specified equal sidelobe level; its transform is equiripple, but the implied endpoint impulses and constant sidelobe floor create practical drawbacks.

§V.I (journal p. 73; PDF p. 23): the prolate-spheroidal criterion maximizes energy inside a selected band for fixed duration and energy; the Kaiser–Bessel window is a simple modified-Bessel approximation parameterized by half the time-bandwidth product.

§V.J (journal pp. 73–76; PDF pp. 23–26): Barcilon–Temes minimizes weighted out-of-band energy for fixed duration and area, placing its behavior between Dolph–Chebyshev minimax and Kaiser–Bessel energy-concentration designs.

§VI, Figs. 57–59 (journal p. 76; PDF p. 26): a 1.0-amplitude tone at bin 10 and a 0.01-amplitude tone at bin 16 are perfectly separated by a rectangular window when both are bin centered; shifting the strong tone to 10.5 bins makes its sidelobes completely hide the −40 dB tone.

§VI, Figs. 62–70 (journal pp. 77–78; PDF pp. 27–28): Hann gives only a marginal 3 dB inter-peak null, Blackman about 17 dB, minimum three-term Blackman–Harris about 20 dB, and the selected four-term Blackman–Harris cleanly resolves both tones with sidelobes below the plotted −70 dB floor.

§VI, Figs. 78–86 (journal pp. 79–80; PDF pp. 29–30): Poisson, Hann–Poisson, and Cauchy families fail the unequal-tone experiment because broad main lobes and/or high sidelobes swamp the weak line; their poor behavior was anticipated by the ENBW-versus-3 dB-bandwidth diagnostic.

§VI, Figs. 90–94 (journal pp. 80–81; PDF pp. 30–31): Dolph–Chebyshev resolves the weak tone but its uniform sidelobes add coherently and are sensitive to strong-tone bin placement, making the apparent floor and relative amplitude unstable.

§VI, Figs. 95–101 (journal pp. 81–82; PDF pp. 31–32): Kaiser–Bessel and Barcilon–Temes strongly resolve the weak tone; Kaiser–Bessel maintains roughly a 20 dB inter-lobe null while holding leakage more than 70 dB down for an appropriate parameter.

§VII (journal pp. 81–82; PDF pp. 31–32): maximum multitone dynamic range requires a concentrated central lobe plus very low sidelobes. Harris judges Kaiser–Bessel, Blackman–Harris, Dolph–Chebyshev, and Barcilon–Temes broadly comparable, with practical advantages to Kaiser–Bessel and Blackman–Harris.

§VII (journal p. 82; PDF p. 32): Harris’s practical recommendation is the four-term Blackman–Harris or four-sample Kaiser–Bessel approximation because a few coefficients suffice and the window can be applied as a short convolution after the DFT.
Appendix (journal p. 83; PDF p. 33): substituting the inverse Fourier representation of f into the windowed finite sum and interchanging sum and integral yields F_w(ω)=F(ω)*W(ω).
pedagogy: Harris teaches by making window choice a detection-and-estimation problem rather than a catalog of tapers. The article first fixes the half-open-record and DFT-even conventions, then gives two equivalent intuitions for leakage: boundary mismatch in a periodic extension and nonlocal projection onto windowed basis vectors. Each figure of merit is derived from a matched-filter or spectral-filter viewpoint and consolidated in a comparative table. The long catalog alternates time-domain definitions, transform shapes, endpoint smoothness, and quantitative metrics, so formulas are always tied to consequences. Section VI then functions as a laboratory: the same two sinusoids—40 dB apart and 5.5 bins separated—are processed by every family, making hidden tones, false nulls, coherent sidelobe addition, and main-lobe encroachment directly comparable. The style is mathematically constructive rather than theorem-proof, with equations, design criteria, and controlled plots but no exercises. Prerequisites are Fourier series/transforms, sampled sinusoids, DFT/FFT, convolution, white-noise expectations, decibels, matched filtering, and basic approximation/optimization ideas. A modern lesson should keep the experimental progression but correct OCR-era notation and explicitly use the modern name ‘Hann’ (Harris notes that ‘Hanning’ merely reflects contemporary conventional usage).

gems: Leakage is not caused by sampling. Harris pins it on finite observation: an off-basis sinusoid does not join smoothly to its periodic copy, so the boundary discontinuity spreads energy across every basis vector. [§III, journal pp. 52–53/PDF pp. 2–3]

The paper’s most persistent implementation warning is a sign error: shifting a centered Hann window to the DFT origin makes its neighboring spectral-convolution coefficients negative. The commonly copied all-positive three-bin formula is wrong. [§V.C, journal p. 62/PDF p. 12]

Harris separates ‘even’ from ‘DFT-even’ with the missing endpoint. A sequence can look asymmetric on the stored grid yet project to zero on every sampled sine basis vector. [§II, Figs. 1–3, journal p. 52/PDF p. 2]

ENBW has a physical picture: replace the window transform by a rectangle with the same peak power gain and choose its width so both collect the same white-noise power. [§IV.A, Fig. 7, journal p. 54/PDF p. 4]

The reciprocal link between normalized ENBW and processing gain turns window choice into a noise-budget decision: every wider equivalent filter admits more noise and loses matched-filter SNR. [§IV.B, journal pp. 54–56/PDF pp. 4–6]

The familiar 3 dB resolution rule fails for coherent DFT addition. Two equal kernels need to cross below one half amplitude, so Harris uses their 6 dB bandwidth as the just-resolved spacing. [§IV.G, Fig. 11, journal pp. 57–58/PDF pp. 7–8]

Worst-case detection loss is surprisingly boring: almost all usable windows lie near 3–4 dB for one tone in broadband noise. The interesting choice begins only when another tone is nearby. [§IV.E and §VII, journal pp. 57, 81/PDF pp. 7, 31]

The triangle window’s doubled transform roots are called a wasteful use of polynomial order: extra zeros are stacked where the response is already zero instead of being placed near sidelobe peaks. [§V.B, journal pp. 59–60/PDF pp. 9–10]

Fejér’s window construction begins as a numerical idea rather than a spectral one: average oscillatory Fourier partial sums so their errors cancel, and the resulting coefficient weights form a triangle. [§V.B, Fig. 15, journal p. 60/PDF p. 10]

The rounded Blackman can outperform the ‘exact’ Blackman far from the main lobe: rounding makes the endpoint coefficients sum to zero, improving asymptotic falloff from 6 to 18 dB/octave. [§V.E, journal p. 64/PDF p. 14]

The smoothness rule is a compact design diagnostic: every additional continuous endpoint derivative buys another power of frequency in far-sidelobe decay. [§§III and V.F, journal pp. 52–53, 65–69/PDF pp. 2–3, 15–19]

Gaussian optimality comes with an honest caveat: it uniquely minimizes the mean-square time-bandwidth product, but a usable finite window must truncate it and thereby surrender the exact optimum. [§V.G, journal pp. 69–71/PDF pp. 19–21]

Dolph–Chebyshev looks superb in the scalar comparison chart yet underperforms in the multitone experiment because its equal sidelobes add coherently and react strongly to coefficient error and bin placement. [§VI–VII, journal pp. 80–82/PDF pp. 30–32]

The entire 33-page survey pivots on one deliberately tiny signal: amplitude 0.01 at bin 16 beside amplitude 1 at bin 10 or 10.5. A half-bin shift changes ‘perfectly visible’ into ‘completely hidden’ under the rectangular window. [§VI, Figs. 57–59, journal p. 76/PDF p. 26]

Hann only gives the −40 dB tone a marginal 3 dB separating null; Blackman gives 17 dB; a selected four-term Blackman–Harris gives about 19 dB while pushing sidelobes below −70 dB. [§VI, Figs. 62, 66, 69, journal pp. 77–78/PDF pp. 27–28]

More sidelobe suppression is not monotonically better: in both cos^α and Gaussian sweeps, widening the main lobe eventually encroaches on the weak tone and makes the separating null shallower. [§VI, journal pp. 77, 79–80/PDF pp. 27, 29–30]

A single scalar chart cannot crown a window. Harris explicitly tells readers that Fig. 12 contains much information ‘but not the full story’; coherent sidelobe structure in Section VI reverses some apparent rankings. [§IV.G and §VII, journal pp. 58, 82/PDF pp. 8, 32]

Harris’s final preference is candid rather than absolute: Kaiser–Bessel wins for easy coefficient generation and a simple time-bandwidth/sidelobe tradeoff, while four-term Blackman–Harris is recommended alongside it for short post-DFT convolution. [§VII, journal p. 82/PDF p. 32]

The spectral-analysis conclusions transfer directly to spatial arrays: replacing time samples with sensor positions turns windowing into aperture shading and the DFT into FFT beamforming. [§VII, journal p. 82/PDF p. 32]
